final_answer:
**No. Idempotency keys make retries safe only for a bounded window, and neither Stripe nor AWS documents them as safe indefinitely.** Stripe says to stop retrying an unresolved operation after 24 hours. AWS says it is "impractical to retain that knowledge indefinitely." AWS's EC2 docs I read give no numeric expiry for client tokens.

I used six of the eight allowed retrievals. I did not use the deep-research skill's subagent and file workflow, because you ruled out shell commands and local files. I researched directly instead.

**Stripe (API v1)**

- Stripe keeps keys for at least 24 hours and may remove them after that. Reusing a removed key can run a new request.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
  - https://docs.stripe.com/error-low-level
- Stripe tells you to limit retries of an unresolved operation to the first 24 hours, with the same key and parameters.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/error-low-level
- If the outcome is still unknown after 24 hours, Stripe says not to retry with the old key or a new one. Reconcile instead: retrieve the object, check the Dashboard, and use webhook events. If that doesn't settle it, contact Stripe support.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/error-low-level
- Keys can be up to 255 characters.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- Reusing a key with different parameters returns an error.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- Stripe saves a result only once endpoint execution begins. Validation failures and concurrent-request conflicts aren't saved, so you can retry those.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- Once execution has begun, Stripe replays the saved response, including `500` errors. A saved `400` is replayed too.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
  - https://docs.stripe.com/error-low-level
- A `500` leaves the outcome indeterminate. Stripe says not to retry with a new key until you've resolved what happened to the original.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/error-low-level
- Stripe's v2 API has different replay behavior and a 30-day window, so the 24-hour figure applies to v1 only.
  - https://docs.stripe.com/error-low-level
- I did not open the v2 page itself, so I haven't checked those v2 details.

**AWS**

- AWS prefers a caller-supplied request identifier. It aims to return a semantically equivalent response for the same identifier "for some interval." That is an interval, not forever.
  - https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/
- AWS says "it's impractical to retain that knowledge indefinitely." For EC2 instances, it describes retention as the resource's lifetime plus an interval, and says retention varies by service.
  - https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/
- This is a design article, not a service SLA. The EC2 developer guide page I read gives no numeric expiry for client tokens, so I can't give an AWS equivalent of Stripe's 24 hours.
  - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html
- An EC2 client token is a case-sensitive string of up to 64 ASCII characters.
  - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html
- Reusing a token with different parameters fails with `IdempotentParameterMismatch`, apart from Region or Availability Zone differences.
  - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html
- EC2 idempotency is scoped to a Region, or to an Availability Zone for zonal requests. The same token in another Region or zone can run again.
  - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html
- Only some EC2 actions support client tokens, so idempotency is not universal.
  - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html
- For EC2 `5xx` responses, AWS recommends retrying "with an appropriate backoff strategy." It says not to retry `4xx` responses, with one exception: a resource that is changing state might succeed on retry.
  - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html
- AWS says "APIs with side effects aren't safe to retry unless they provide idempotency." That makes idempotency necessary, but it doesn't make unlimited retries safe.
  - https://builder.aws.com/content/3EumjoZascWd1oZiEgL8ORlv3qE/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter
- AWS separately says retries cost the server capacity. It warns that independent retries at each layer can multiply load (its example is 243x). It advises limiting retries, for example with a local token bucket, and using backoff and jitter. This is a load argument, which idempotency doesn't address.
  - https://builder.aws.com/content/3EumjoZascWd1oZiEgL8ORlv3qE/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter
- The AWS idempotency article does not discuss retry limits or backoff.
  - https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/

**What the evidence doesn't settle**

- I found no numeric token-retention period for AWS services. It varies by service, and I only checked EC2 and the Builders' Library articles.
- This is a comparison of Stripe's explicit 24-hour guidance and AWS's less specific design guidance. They aren't like-for-like numeric limits.
